opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it started a bit by accident. I'd spent years working in areas like algebraic geometry and the mathematical side of logic and category theory, and I'd become increasingly aware that deep learning was this enormous phenomenon that I didn't understand at all. Like a lot of mathematicians, my first instinct was to look for the theory that explained why it worked, and I found that the classical statistical learning theory story didn't really hold together for neural networks. The models are hugely overparameterized, they generalize anyway, and the standard tools based on counting parameters or assuming the loss landscape looks locally like a nice quadratic bowl just don't describe what's going on.

Then I came across Watanabe's book, *Algebraic Geometry and Statistical Learning Theory*, and it was a strange moment of recognition. Here was someone who had taken seriously the fact that models like neural networks are *singular*: the map from parameters to the functions they compute is far from one-to-one, the Fisher information matrix is degenerate, and the set of parameters that achieve the best possible fit isn't a point but a complicated geometric object with singularities. Watanabe's insight was that you can't paper over that degeneracy. It's the main event. To handle it he brought in resolution of singularities, Hironaka's theorem, which is about as central a tool as there is in my home field.

What really hooked me was that the geometry isn't just a technical obstacle; it carries the answer. The key invariant in the theory, the real log canonical threshold, or learning coefficient, measures how singular the set of good parameters is, and that quantity governs things like the Bayesian free energy and the generalization error. So in place of the naive parameter count, you get an effective measure of model complexity that comes from the geometry of the loss landscape. Roughly speaking, more degenerate solutions are effectively simpler, and the Bayesian posterior prefers them. That gives you a principled way to think about why overparameterized models might prefer solutions that generalize.

For an algebraic geometer, that's an irresistible bridge. The concepts I'd spent my life studying, like singularities, blow-ups, and birational invariants, turned out to be precisely the language needed to describe something important about learning machines. And there's a further hope that motivates a lot of what we do now: if the structure a network learns is reflected in the geometry of its loss landscape, then studying that geometry, and how it changes over training, might tell us about the internal structure the model is developing. That connects to interpretability and ultimately to alignment, which is a big part of why I think this is worth working on right now, not just as beautiful mathematics but as something that might help us understand the systems we're building.

r001.rationale: The response presents algebraic geometry and resolution of singularities as central to Watanabe’s theory, and explains that the geometric invariant governs Bayesian free energy and posterior preference.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the honest answer is that it was partly accident and partly a kind of recognition. I'd spent most of my career in algebraic geometry, working on things like matrix factorizations and derived categories, which is about as far from machine learning as you can get on the surface. But around 2017, 2018, I started paying serious attention to deep learning, partly because of the AI safety concerns and partly just because it was clear something important was happening that mathematicians weren't really engaging with.

And when I started reading the theory literature, I had this nagging feeling that the standard tools weren't quite the right ones. A lot of classical statistical learning theory assumes the models are what Watanabe calls regular, meaning roughly that the map from parameters to the function the model computes is nicely behaved, with a well-defined Fisher information matrix that's invertible. Neural networks violate that in a very fundamental way. There are many different parameter settings that compute the same function, and the loss landscape around those sets is degenerate. It's not a bowl, it's something much more complicated.

Then I came across Watanabe's book, and the thing that struck me was that he had understood this problem decades earlier and had attacked it with exactly the tools I knew. He realized that the set of parameters that minimize the loss is, generically, a singular algebraic variety, and that the right way to understand the asymptotics of Bayesian learning is through resolution of singularities, Hironaka's theorem, and zeta functions. The key invariant, the real log canonical threshold, is a quantity straight out of birational geometry. So for me it was this surprising moment of finding that a deep piece of the mathematics I cared about was already sitting at the heart of the question of how these systems learn.

I think what really hooked me, though, was that it wasn't just an aesthetic coincidence. The geometry actually has content. The learning coefficient tells you something about effective complexity that's quite different from counting parameters, and it gives you a way to think about why a model with far more parameters than data points can still generalize. Singularities are, in a sense, where the interesting structure lives, and degeneracy is a feature rather than a nuisance. Once you see it that way, it's hard to go back to thinking about these systems in the regular paradigm.

r001.rationale: The response says Watanabe’s Bayesian learning asymptotics are understood through resolution of singularities and zeta functions, and identifies the real log canonical threshold as an invariant from birational geometry.

astra-6.text:
What drew me in was that the geometry seemed to be doing real explanatory work. In algebraic geometry, we study singularities—places where a space fails to look locally like a smooth manifold. And in neural networks, those aren’t exceptional cases you can conveniently ignore. They’re built into the way the models are parametrized: many different choices of weights can represent the same function.

That matters because a lot of classical statistical theory assumes, roughly speaking, that you can identify a parameter from the distribution it describes, and that the loss looks like a nice quadratic near an optimum. For neural networks, those assumptions fail. Watanabe’s theory takes that failure seriously and uses algebraic geometry to work out what replaces the classical picture.

The particularly compelling thing is that you get a connection between the geometry of those singularities and statistical quantities like generalization error. The effective complexity of a model isn’t simply its number of parameters. It depends on the structure of the space of parameters that fit the data.

So here was a setting where mathematics that might otherwise seem quite abstract could help explain something genuinely puzzling: how these enormously overparametrized systems can nevertheless learn useful things. That was a very attractive invitation to an algebraic geometer.

r001.rationale: The response says Watanabe’s theory uses algebraic geometry to analyze singularities and connect them to generalization error, but it does not identify Bayesian statistics as the setting or state algebraic geometry’s role in it.

sol-6.1.text:
What drew me in was the possibility that algebraic geometry could tell us something substantive about how neural networks learn. In classical statistics, you often assume that a parameter uniquely identifies a model and that the loss looks locally like a quadratic bowl. But neural networks violate those assumptions in quite fundamental ways. Many different parameter settings can represent the same function, and the geometry around a minimum can be much more complicated.

Watanabe’s theory takes that singular structure seriously. Rather than treating it as a technical nuisance, it makes it central to the statistical analysis. And the tools that appear—things like resolution of singularities—are tools from algebraic geometry. So there was this striking connection between mathematics I knew and questions about learning and generalization.

The attraction wasn’t just that there was some geometry involved. It was that the geometry could determine quantities with statistical meaning. That suggested a route toward understanding why these very large, highly redundant models behave as they do, even when the usual parameter-counting intuition seems inadequate.

r001.rationale: The response says algebraic-geometric tools help analyze singular structure and yield statistically meaningful quantities, but it does not identify their role specifically in Bayesian statistics as a core tenet.
